fields.title: Channels: not "where everyone is", but where your user is already solving this problem
fields.keyTakeaway: You choose a channel based on where people are already looking for a solution, and test it with a small bid. A channel that works for a neighbor says nothing about yours: they have a different product, different pricing, and a different decision cycle.
fields.checkQuestion: A competitor grew on paid search. Why is this a weak argument for starting with it?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **where and how to acquire consumers?**
fields.blocks/1/text: End-to-end domain example: Reestr is a fictional electronic document management service for small business: invoices, certificates, signatures. Subscription model, 14-day free trial. In module M1, we figured out who we speak to and what we say; here, we focus on how this creates a steady stream of clients.
fields.blocks/2/text: **What happens if you do not answer the question.** The budget goes to where "everyone hangs out". A quarter later, there is reach, no clients, and it is unclear whether the channel or the offer is at fault.
fields.blocks/3/items/0: **Intent** — is the user already searching for a solution, or are you interrupting them? Search is intent, a feed is interruption. These carry different costs and copy.
fields.blocks/3/items/1: **Reachability** — can you actually separate your audience from everyone else? "Small business" is not targeting; "people searching 'how to issue a VAT invoice'" is targeting.
fields.blocks/3/items/2: **Cycle** — how much time passes between the first touchpoint and the decision? If it's two weeks, a channel cannot be evaluated in one week.
fields.blocks/3/items/3: **Bid test:** minimal budget, single offer, fixed timeframe, and a predefined threshold for what lead cost signals "it failed".
fields.blocks/4/text: **The offer matters more than the channel.** The same channel yields different costs with different promises. Therefore, test copy variations within a fixed channel first, and only then compare channels against each other.
fields.blocks/5/text:
Search for "how to issue an invoice for sole proprietor" — signup cost 340 ₽, every fifth person reaches payment.
Targeted ads for "business owners" on social media — 210 ₽ per signup, one in thirty reaches payment. Cheap at the start, expensive at the end.
Partnership with an accounting service — 8 clients per month without a budget, but contract negotiation took six weeks.
Industry channel in a messenger — 3 clients, but all of them pay for a second month.

The takeaway is not "search is better", but "you need to compare channels by paid conversions, not by signups".
fields.blocks/6/text: A cheap channel is usually narrow: its capacity runs out and costs rise. That is why a growing product always searches for a second channel — before the first reaches its limit, not after.
fields.blocks/6/title: A single channel rarely scales indefinitely
fields.blocks/7/text: Channels don't fix the product. If users churn in week two, any new channel just pours water faster into a leaky bucket — and does so at a higher cost.
